title: Granny cluster — three trebles into a chain space
subtitle: The building block of every granny square
excerpt: The granny cluster is three trebles worked into a chain space, all sharing the same open base. It is the single technique behind every granny square, granny stripe, and granny hexagon. Learn this and the rest of the granny family follows.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 1 (1886) — the granny square worked with treble clusters into chain spaces. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776 — cluster stitches in circular motifs.

glossaryTerms.definition: Three trebles worked into the same chain space, all separate (not joined at the top). The granny-square motif is built from groups of granny clusters separated by ch-2 spaces at corners and ch-1 spaces at sides.

content.text: is three trebles into the same chain space. Each treble is worked individually and completely — unlike a bobble or cluster where partial stitches are joined at the top. The granny cluster's three trebles stand side by side, all pulling from the open chain space below. This openness is what gives granny-square fabric its characteristic lightness.
The difference from a standard cluster

A treble cluster joins multiple incomplete trebles at the top — the tops converge. A granny cluster works three complete trebles, each fully closed, all into the same space — the tops stay separate. The result looks like a small neat row of three, not a converging dome. In granny-square patterns written in UK shorthand: '3 tr into ch sp' means a granny cluster.
Position the hook at the chain space where the cluster goes.
Insert the hook under all the chains of the chain space — not into one specific chain, but into the open gap below all of them.
Work 1 tr. Then work another tr into the same space. Then a third tr. All three go into the same open space.
The three trebles stand side by side: one granny cluster made.
Make a magic ring or ch 4 and sl st to first ch to form a small ring.
Round 1: ch 3 (counts as first tr). Work 2 more tr into the ring (first cluster). Ch 2 (corner space). *(3 tr into ring, ch 2) 3 more times. Sl st to top of ch-3 to join. (4 clusters, 4 ch-2 corners)

Round 2: sl st across to first corner ch-2 sp. Ch 3, 2 tr into corner sp, ch 2, 3 tr into same corner sp (corner cluster pair with ch-2 between). Ch 1. *(3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr) into next corner sp, ch 1; repeat from * twice. Sl st to top of ch-3. (8 clusters, 4 ch-1 sides, 4 ch-2 corners)

attrs.title: The corner is always (3tr, ch 2, 3tr)
attrs.body: Every corner of every round is two granny clusters separated by a ch-2 space, both worked into the same corner ch-2 space. The ch-2 is the turning point. Missing it makes a circle; adding extra stitches makes a ruffled edge. The side clusters are single groups of 3 tr with ch-1 between.

items.cause: Too many stitches per round, particularly at the corners
items.fix: Each corner is exactly (3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr) — no more. Count the clusters per round: each new round adds 4 side clusters, one per side.

items.cause: Chain foundation ring left loose, or magic ring not pulled tight
items.fix: If using a chain ring, close the magic ring as an alternative — it pulls completely shut. If using a chain ring, pull the starting tail firmly after completing round 1.

content.text: Add a second round of colour for a classic two-tone granny square. Join-as-you-go connects granny squares as you complete the final round of each motif, avoiding the separate sewing-up stage. The granny hexagon uses six granny clusters in round 1 rather than four.
